slide_text: Pattern Matching -- Inventing Wildcards and Regular Expressions When you type in a file browser, or validate an email address on a signup form, or grep through a server log -- a pattern matcher is at work. In this chapter you will invent one from scratch: first exact matching, then the wildcard, then the surprisingly deep wildcard (a beautiful use of the recursion you already own), and finally you will graduate to Python's industrial-strength module and mine a real web-server log with it. Quick Check 3.1 -- Why `*` Needs Backtracking The pattern is matched against the string . The is greedy -- it first tries to consume as many characters as possible. Why does the matcher need backtracking to find the correct match? A. Because can only match letters, not or B. The greedy initially consumes , but then the final in the pattern has nothing left to match -- so the matcher must back up and try consuming fewer characters C. Backtracking is needed because the string contains duplicate characters D. The pattern is invalid -- must be at the end Answer: B. The greedily eats everything, but then the at the end of the pattern has no characters left to match. The matcher must "back up" (backtrack) and let the consume fewer characters until the remaining pattern can match.

What you just invented: The branching trick in your matcher -- try both, succeed if either succeeds -- is called backtracking . It is the same idea that solves mazes, Sudoku, and the N-Queens problem, and it is exactly how simple regex engines are implemented.
